extracted.intended_audience: OGP member governments, regulators, policy-makers, civil society organizations, and reformers working on open regulatory processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and measurable indicators for making regulatory rulemaking open, transparent, participatory, and contestable across four areas: access to laws, transparency of rulemaking, public consultation (notice-and-comment), and mechanisms to challenge regulations. Includes maturity-model actions, measurement questions (GIRG), and examples from OGP countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessing laws and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the private sector and general public have free and effective access to the entire (official) collection of reliably updated and complete national laws and regulations of a jurisdiction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a comprehensive, searchable, free-of-charge central website (or equivalent), eliminate data-usage restrictions, publish primary and secondary texts, ensure updates and local-level disclosure; be mindful that availability does not guarantee quality (e.g., completeness, accuracy, official consolidated versions).

rubrics_metrics.name: GIRG assessment questions for publication of laws and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The GIRG assesses publication/accessibility by asking: Are primary laws in a single place? If yes, how accessed? Are secondary regulations codified and in a single place? If yes, how accessed? Are these websites/registries free to access? Are they updated systemically?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers form a picture of availability; caveat that GIRG does not measure downstream data quality (usability, accuracy, machine-readability) or whether published information is complete or official.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity model — Unified website / centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a comprehensive and free-of-charge unified website containing all existing legislation and regulatory texts (including, where relevant, case law and local-level norms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure interoperability so citizens can access laws, regulations and related materials in one place; where full online publication is not feasible, provide centralized alternatives (see gazettes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity model — Searchable information and categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Online systems should enable categorization and searching of laws and regulations by type, geographic region, agency, legislative area, and sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make legal repositories user-friendly and searchable to facilitate compliance and public use; consider structured metadata to support search and linkage across documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity model — Regular updates
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep all regulatory and legal repositories up to date so that published collections reflect the law currently in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systemically update websites/registries to avoid publication of outdated or unofficial versions; where publication in the gazette is required for enforceability, reflect that status clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity model — Data reuse and machine-readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitate reuse of legal/regulatory data by eliminating licensing and other restrictions and ensuring machine-readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish laws and regulations in open, machine-readable formats and with permissive reuse terms (no restrictive copyright/licensing) to enable analysis, reuse and technological access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maturity model — Journals and gazettes as complementary mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: If funding or technical capacity for online publication is limited, governments should make laws accessible through printed journals and official gazettes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gazettes are particularly important where internet penetration is low and (in many countries) publication in the gazette affects enforceability; preferably, publish gazettes online and free of charge as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of rulemaking (public notice and publication of proposed texts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are officials systematically obligated to issue timely public notice of proposed changes in regulations and to publish proposed texts for public review and comment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish forward regulatory plans and draft texts on unified portals that enable feedback; ensure regulators provide timely notice, publish regulatory development timelines, and enable citizens to follow a regulation from development through adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish forward regulatory plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should publish forward regulatory plans containing planned laws and regulatory initiatives (ideally annually and ahead of the legislative/regulatory cycle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward plans should be publicly available (example: Spain's legal obligation to publish a forward plan prior to the year of enactment); publishing plans helps citizens anticipate and engage in upcoming rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public consultation / notice-and-comment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there minimum standards relating to how, when, and from whom policy-makers seek input on new or amended regulations before issuing final regulations (i.e., notice-and-comment)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt laws or binding rules that mandate notice-and-comment, set minimum standards (e.g., minimum consultation periods, publication of drafts), require outreach to affected groups, and provide oversight mechanisms to monitor compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to consultations and providing reasoned responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Do regulators document public input and provide reasoned responses to comments prior to adoption of final regulations (e.g., consolidated responses or summaries showing which comments were taken into account)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce consolidated response documents, publish summaries/tables linking comments to dispositions, and ensure consultation results are publicly accessible (examples: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denmark, Estonia, Spain, Canada). Exclude commercially sensitive or privacy-protected material as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early engagement and minimum requirements for consultation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultations should seek early engagement with affected communities and adhere to minimum quality standards for transparency, inclusiveness, and documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines can set minimum requirements (e.g., early engagement, targeted outreach, minimum notice periods, centralized portals for consultations) and be legally binding or policy instruments to improve practice across government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenging regulations (access to judicial/administrative review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Can citizens challenge the legal validity of a regulation or challenge actions/decisions of regulators under a regulation (procedural and substantive grounds)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt legal provisions that provide a basis to challenge regulations developed without open processes or if discriminatory; publish information about the challenge process and ensure remedies are accessible (cover both procedural and substantive review where possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: OGP action plans and IRM evaluation metrics (ambition, completion, early results, co-creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: OGP action plans should be co-created with citizens and are evaluated by the Independent Reporting Mechanism (IRM) using metrics such as ambition (stretch beyond baseline), completion (implementation), early results (concrete changes), and quality of co-creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design commitments to be ambitious, monitor implementation and early results, document co-creation processes and public influence; note IRM findings that strong co-creation of OGP plans is not necessarily correlated with strong government-wide consultation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open policy‑making values and complementary commitment types
rubrics_metrics.description: Open policy-making commitments should advance OGP core values: access to information, civic participation, and public accountability, and may include varied approaches such as issue-specific participatory processes, training/capacity building, legislative openness, lobbying transparency, and e-petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing commitments, consider a mix of disclosure, participatory mechanisms, capacity building, and accountability measures to mainstream open regulatory practices across levels and sectors of government.
